header.name: Lattices in Computer Science
header.description:
A lattice is a dicrete addtive sub-group of an n-dimensional Euclidean space. Lattices have been extensively studied both in computer science and mathematics. Over the last couple of decades lattices have found numerous applications across varied fields like combinatorial optimization, cryptography, algorithms, complexity theory and algebraic number theory.

This course will focus on first building some basic backgroud on n-dimensional Euclidean lattices. This will be followed up by discussing some (believed to be) hard problems on lattices and their associated complexity results. This will be followed by looking at some applications of lattices in areas like combinatorial optimizations (the integer programming problem), number theory and cryptanalysis. Finally we will look at how the lattice-based hardness assumptions can be used to build cryptographic protocols that are secure against quantum adversaries. In particular we will end the course by looking at Regev’s polytime quantum reduction from (worst-case) approximate SIVP to (average-case) LWE.
prerequisites_mandatory: Probability and Statistics (MTH201) (or Probability and Random Process (ECE501))

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Students should be able to learn the basics of lattces, some hard problems on lattices and some related complexity results.

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Students should learn some basic lattice based cryptographic protocols and cryptanalytic techniques.

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Students should be able to appreciate why some of the schemes mentioned in CO2 are post-quantum secure.

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Students should be able to apply the mathematical techniques learnt here, elsewhere.

lecture_topics: Recap: Norm, distance or metirc, inner product space, Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization, definition of module
Lattice definition, fundamental parallelpiped, Unimodular matrix, Determinant of a lattice
Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization – matrix representation, successive minima
Bounds on Successive Minima: Blichfeldt’s Theorem, Blichfeldt’s Theorem, Minkowski’s First Theorem, Minkowski’s Second Theorem
Dual Lattices: Geometric interpretation, dual basis, Two Transference theorems
An application: Fermat’s Theorem on Sums of Two Squares, Hernite normal form (HNF), Basis reduction to HNF
Sub-lattices, Groups, Smith Normal form, Size of elements, sampling elements from finite group
Basis reduction in 2-dimension – Gauss’s Algorithm
LLL-reduction
Applications of LLL algorithm:Low exponent attack on RSA
CVP-problem and Babai’s nearest plane algorithm
SVP-problem, Complexity results for SVP and CVP, Relation between GapSVP and GapCVP
Integer Programming Problem, Lenstra’s Algorithm
Definitions of BPP-class, Arthur-Merlin (AM) class and Co-AM class; Definition of Periodic distributions; The Goldreich-Goldwasser protocol and it’s proof (i.e., GapCVP_{\sqrt{n}} \in NP \cap Co-AM)
A simply exponential algorithm for SVP (Ajtai-Kumar-Sivakumar)
Fourier Transformation – one dimensional and n-dimensional;
Fourier Series – one dimensional and n-dimensional; Poission summation formula;
Dual Lattices; Minkowski’s reduced basis, Korkine Zolotarev Basis (KZ-basis) – Block KZ basis, Hermite KZ basis;
Definition of primitive vector; Lagarias, Lenstra and Schnorr’s result on approximate SVP
Transference Theorem – Bauaszyczyk; Application - GapSVP_{n} \in Co-NP; Coverting radius;
Proof of Bauaszyczyk’s Theorem
Approximate SIVP problem; Smoothing parameter;
Cryptograhic Constructions - Collision resistant hash functions (CRHF) (a.k.a. Ajtai-GGH hash function), Regev’s encryption scheme, etc.
The Learning with Errors (LWE) problem (and it's relation to lattice problems) – Regev’s polytime quantum reduction from approximate SIVP to LWE
